summary: Describes changes to the sockets API, the de facto standard programming interface for TCP/IP applications, that are needed to support IPv6. The goal is to keep the portability applications enjoyed with IPv4. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Programs talk to the network through a standard doorway called sockets. This note describes how that doorway changes so it also works with the newer IPv6 addresses.

questions: what is the ipv6 sockets api
subtitle: How the sockets programming interface was extended so applications can use IPv6 addresses, multicast and name lookup.

tldr.problem: The sockets API exposes the size of an IP address, and IPv6 addresses are 128 bits instead of 32, so existing programs and structures cannot simply carry them.
tldr.mechanism: The memo adds a new address structure (sockaddr_in6), the AF_INET6 family, new socket options, interface-index functions, and protocol-independent lookup and conversion functions such as getaddrinfo() and inet_ntop().
tldr.outcome: IPv4 programs keep working and IPv6 programs can still talk to IPv4 nodes. The memo is informational: the official sockets specification is the POSIX standard it cites.

today: RFC 3493 is an informational document that obsoletes RFC 2553, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself says the official sockets specification is the POSIX standard it cites.

sections.title: Why the Sockets API Had to Change
sections.content:
IPv4 addresses are 32 bits long and IPv6 addresses are 128 bits long. The socket interface makes the address size quite visible to applications, so the parts of the API that expose addresses must change. IPv6 also has new features that need to be reachable from programs.

This memo defines the basic extensions that suit a broad range of applications. More specialized needs, such as raw sockets and access to IPv6 extension headers, are left to a companion document, the advanced API (RFC 2292).

The text says development began in 1994 in the IETF IPng working group, and the API was published first in RFC 2133, then in RFC 2553, and reached its final form here. The memo is informational only; the official specification of the sockets API is the IEEE/Open Group standard it cites.
sections.plainLanguage: Old network programs expect short addresses, like a short phone number. IPv6 addresses are much longer, so the instructions for programs needed an update.

sections.title: Design Goals and What Changes
sections.content:
The design aims to keep existing programs working. API changes should give source and binary compatibility, stay as small as possible, let applications interoperate with both IPv6 and IPv4 hosts without knowing which is which, and keep IPv6 addresses in data structures 64-bit aligned for performance.

The core socket functions such as bind(), connect() and sendto() pass addresses through opaque pointers plus a length, so they do not need to change. What does change is the address data structure, the name-to-address functions (gethostbyname() and gethostbyaddr() are left as they are and new functions are added), the address conversion functions, and a few extras such as the hop limit and multicast options.

The existing sockaddr_in structure has 8 octets of unused space, but still cannot hold a 16-octet IPv6 address together with the family and port. A new structure is required.
sections.plainLanguage: The plan is to change as little as possible, like adding a longer shelf for the new big books while leaving the old shelves alone.

sections.title: IPv6 Address Structures and Compatibility
sections.content:
A new address family AF_INET6 and protocol family PF_INET6 are defined. The in6_addr structure holds one address as sixteen 8-bit elements in network byte order. The sockaddr_in6 structure carries sin6_family, sin6_port, sin6_flowinfo, sin6_addr and sin6_scope_id. A variant with a leading sin6_len field is given for 4.4BSD-based systems, announced by the SIN6_LEN macro.

Applications create IPv6 sockets by passing AF_INET6 to socket(). Systems must keep supporting AF_INET and sockaddr_in, and one process may hold IPv4 and IPv6 sockets at once.

To reach IPv4 nodes, an application can use an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address, written ::FFFF:<IPv4-address>, in a sockaddr_in6. The IPv4 address sits in the low-order 32 bits and the high-order 96 bits hold the fixed prefix. The IN6_IS_ADDR_V4MAPPED() macro tells an application when it needs to know.

Other pieces in this part: the wildcard address (in6addr_any and IN6ADDR_ANY_INIT), the loopback address (in6addr_loopback and IN6ADDR_LOOPBACK_INIT), and struct sockaddr_storage, which is large enough and aligned well enough to hold any supported address structure. The _INIT constants can be used only at declaration time, not in assignments. The IPv4 INADDR_xxx constants are in host byte order, while the IPv6 ones are in network byte order.

The sin6_flowinfo field is not yet specified: applications should set it to zero and ignore it on structures built by the system.
sections.plainLanguage: The new address card is bigger, with room for a longer address. An old-style address can be tucked into a special spot on the new card so old and new computers can still write to each other.

sections.title: Interfaces and Socket Options
sections.content:
Network interfaces are identified by an interface index, a small positive integer starting at 1 (0 is never used). Four functions work with them: if_nametoindex(), if_indextoname(), if_nameindex() and if_freenameindex().

All new socket options use level IPPROTO_IPV6 and the prefix IPV6_. IPV6_UNICAST_HOPS sets the hop limit of outgoing unicast packets: -1 means the kernel default, 0 to 255 is used as given, and any other value gives EINVAL.

For multicast, sending options are IPV6_MULTICAST_IF, IPV6_MULTICAST_HOPS (default 1) and IPV6_MULTICAST_LOOP (default 1). Receiving uses IPV6_JOIN_GROUP and IPV6_LEAVE_GROUP with a struct ipv6_mreq holding the group address and an interface index. A process must join the group to receive datagrams sent to it, and UDP applications must also bind the port.

IPV6_V6ONLY is a boolean option, off by default. When on, an AF_INET6 socket handles IPv6 traffic only. One stated use is running two versions of the same server on the same port, one for IPv6 and one for IPv4.
sections.plainLanguage: Each network plug in a computer gets a number. Special switches let a program say how far its messages may travel and which group chats to join.

sections.title: Name Lookup and Address Conversion
sections.content:
gethostbyname() is inadequate for many programs: the caller cannot say which address types it wants, and many implementations are not thread safe. gethostbyname2() was deprecated in RFC 2553 and is no longer part of the basic API.

The replacement is getaddrinfo(), which takes a node name, a service name and optional hints, and returns a linked list of addrinfo structures. Each entry holds values usable directly in socket() and connect() or bind(). Flags include AI_PASSIVE, AI_CANONNAME, AI_NUMERICHOST, AI_NUMERICSERV, AI_V4MAPPED, AI_ALL and AI_ADDRCONFIG. Results are freed with freeaddrinfo(), and failures use EAI_xxx codes described by gai_strerror(). Both calls must be thread-safe.

The reverse is getnameinfo(), which turns a socket address into a host name and service name, with flags such as NI_NUMERICHOST, NI_NAMEREQD and NI_DGRAM.

inet_pton() and inet_ntop() convert between text and binary forms for both families, replacing inet_addr() and inet_ntoa(). Constants INET_ADDRSTRLEN (16) and INET6_ADDRSTRLEN (46) size the text buffers. A family of macros, such as IN6_IS_ADDR_LOOPBACK() and IN6_IS_ADDR_MULTICAST(), tests for special addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of making you work out the address yourself, one helper function takes a name like a friend's and hands you every working way to reach them.

sections.title: Security, Changes and Status
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section is brief. It says IPv6 provides a number of new security mechanisms that need to be accessible to applications, and that companion memos on socket extensions for IPv6 security were being written.

Compared with RFC 2553, this version adds a history of the API and its relation to the Open Group/IEEE/ISO standard, removes getipnodebyname() and getipnodebyaddr() in favor of getaddrinfo() and getnameinfo(), adds the IPV6_V6ONLY option, and defers the full definition of sin6_flowinfo to a future specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The note says safety tools for IPv6 will need their own instructions, which were still being written.

items.title: Compatibility
items.text: Existing programs keep working, both as binaries and when recompiled.

items.title: Small changes
items.text: Keep API changes minimal to ease converting IPv4 applications.

items.title: Interoperate
items.text: Applications should work with IPv6 and IPv4 hosts without knowing which.

items.title: Alignment
items.text: IPv6 addresses in structures are 64-bit aligned for speed.
